title: Tale of the Merchant and His Sons

keywords: tale of the merchant and his sons
full_text:
Bakhtiyar recounted the story of an affluent merchant of Isfahan who had three sons:

'Feeling his strength failing, the merchant called his three sons to his bedchamber, divided his fortune into three equal parts of ten thousand dinars, and said: "Go forth into the world, and in three years, return to show me how you have employed your inheritance."

The eldest son went to the capital, bought a magnificent palace, filled it with sixty servants, and gave sumptuous banquets every evening, boasting: "I am enjoying the fruits of my father’s labor!" Within two years, his gold was spent, his flattering friends vanished, and he was reduced to begging in rags.

The second son, fearing to lose his gold, dug a deep pit beneath his cellar floor, buried his ten thousand dinars, and sat above it with a cudgel, starving himself on stale crusts in perpetual anxiety. His gold neither grew nor fed a hungry soul.

The youngest son, Farhad, took his portion and invested it in knowledge and production: he purchased barren hillside land, dug irrigation canals from the mountain river, planted ten thousand olive trees and almond saplings, and established an agricultural craft school for poor youths of the district.

At the end of three years, the three sons returned to their father.

The eldest stood in rags; the second produced his rusted, useless gold; but Farhad led his father to the mountain slope, showing him thriving green orchards laden with fruit, water flowing in clean canals, and a hundred young artisans singing at their work!

The father embraced Farhad with tears of joy, saying: "You alone understood the true end of affairs! Gold buried in stone is dead, and gold spent on vanity is poison; but wealth invested in knowledge, labor, and the welfare of others lives forever."'
moral: True wealth is not gold to be spent, but knowledge and productive skills that sustain future generations.
